To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the liver of rats with experimental alcohol‐induc ed liver disease shows enhanced lipid peroxidat ion and decreased hepatic antioxidant factors, and that these alterations are associated with oxidative damage to proteins.

chronic alcohol consumption in the rat induces fatty liver and necro‐inflammatory liver lesions, and that these lesions are associated with enhanced lipid peroxidations, decreased antioxidant factors and protein damage.
chronic ethanol feeding induces lipid peroxidation (LPO), impairs the antioxidant potential of the liver and induces oxidative damage to proteins.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of lipid and protein oxidation in alcohol‐induced hepatic damage.
a better understanding of the mechanisms of alcohol‐induced oxidative stress and its role in the pathogenesis of alcoholic liver damage.
the role of free radicals in ethanol‐induced liver injury and the mechanisms by which they are generated.

chronic ethanol feeding induces lipid peroxidation with a consequent depletion of the major antioxidant factors, and protein oxidation, which may play a significant role in the pathogenesis of alcohol‐induced hepatic injury.
the ethanol‐related oxidative stress in this model is associated with liver pathology.
chronic ethanol consumption induces liver injury through a mechanism that involves oxidative stress.

alcohol‐related oxidative stress is associated with protein and enzyme damage.
chronic alcohol intake leads to an increase in oxidative stress and that this increase is associated with a significant decrease in the antioxidant potential.
